findings: Scale solves who holds what; it does not solve who you is. The atlas includes 26 pretrained bases from 1B to ~1T parameters (Llama-3.1 405B, Kimi-K2, DeepSeek-V3 and V4, MiMo-V2.5 and V2.5-Pro, Trinity-Large, Qwen2.5 72B, Gemma-4, GLM-4 and others). On the 3rd-person twin of the shortcut-free you query, their accuracy rises with scale, to .72–.99 at ≥30B. On this accuracy test, the 0-shot you version stays at .15–.33, around the 29% chance line, with no trend in size. The swap shift of Figure 2 is a different measure. From 14B up, it reads weakly positive in 10 of the 11 bases with a public size.

The items are unambiguous. An independent solver reads only the prompt text. Its rules: I is the speaker, and you is the named addressee, or the other person in a two-person chat. It finds a unique answer for every one of the 900 deixis items and 540 twins. Every answer matches the gold label. The cleanest contrast is I against you on the same transcripts, with the same format, bookkeeping and question: bases ≥30B score .21–.60 on “I'm holding the” and .15–.33 on “you're holding the”. Part of the gap to the 3rd-person twin is the cost of tracking the transcript. The I version pays that cost too. The part that belongs to you alone is about .2.

Bases bind I to the speaker and leave you unbound. A speaker-swap test changes only the name on the last line of a two-person chat (“Neil: Right now you're holding the” → “Kevin: …”), which flips the right answer. Here the test runs on scenes where objects change hands, on 18 bases from 9B to about 1T parameters. For “I'm holding the”, all 18 bases tested move their answer with the speaker given three examples (+.14 to +.58 in gold probability), and 17 of 18 already do at 0-shot (+.06 to +.17; Kimi-K2 +.03). For “you're holding the”, 11 of 18 do not move at 0-shot (within ±.04). Three move the wrong way and read you as the speaker (Gemma-2 9B, Gemma-4 31B, OLMo-3 32B). Four of the largest move slightly the right way (DeepSeek-V3 +.07, DeepSeek-V4 Flash +.10, Kimi-K2 +.05, Llama-3.1 405B +.05), a fraction of their I shift with examples. In bases of this size, the failure is therefore mostly an unattached you, not a misread speaker. Smaller bases read below zero on the same test (Figure 2).

The residual signal comes from the shortcut. On all structural-you items 405B scores 32%, just over chance. Restricted to items where the answer is neither the last-mentioned person nor the last speaker, it scores 21%, and the remaining errors point the wrong way. The Shortcut-free toggle shows the drop.

The reflex/deliberate split holds across vendors, and the reflex error has one direction. Asked for only the next word, frontier models score 21–48% on structural you, against about 29% by chance (all items, 0-shot: GPT-5.5 48%, GPT-5 mini 30%, Grok 4.3 33%, DeepSeek V3.2 21%). Allowed to reason, they reach 100%, 96%, 89% and 70%. Most reflex misses pick the speaker's own object, reading “you're holding” as “I'm holding”. For open bases of 9B and up, the speaker-swap test shows mostly non-binding rather than inversion. Each deixis cell opens its error anatomy.

Frontier models resolve the referent and name it. Asked to finish a line spoken to the person holding the object, GPT-5.5 names that person every time instead of saying you. The answer columns use referent scoring (the name counts as correct) and show how often the seat form (you/me) appears. On these columns the answer is a person, not an object. There, frontier models resolve the referent ~100% of the time on reflex. In a frame ablation the deliberate frame (“work out the answer”) biases answers toward names, and GPT-5.5 still names the asker when told “you are Ted”.

More tokens and anneals grow bookkeeping, not perspective. Three training runs are measured at two or more points: Trinity-Large TrueBase (10T tokens, pre-anneal) → Base (17T, with anneals); OLMo-3 32B stage 1 → final; OLMo-2 7B from 2.9T tokens through mid-training. The later checkpoints gain code aliasing at 0-shot (copy-then-mutate: Trinity 36 → 98, OLMo-3 3 → 35; rebind: OLMo-3 14 → 69) and set binding (OLMo-3 45 → 76). Two-person you stays at or below the 29% chance line throughout (Trinity 21 → 17, OLMo-3 23 → 29, OLMo-2 27 → 22).

A human reader solves these on reflex. The human row reads every item cold, once, without options, and is at ceiling on the perspective columns where 405B is at chance. It is one reader and a handful of items per cell: a reference point, not an estimate.
gaps: 3-shot (same type) shows how much a model takes from examples of the test item's own type. On the aliased-list columns, those examples show the answer's role, so these cells read how well a model copies that role. In a check on eight models, the examples' answers were flipped to the wrong role. Every model that had gained 20 points or more from the examples then fell to near zero (Qwen2.5-7B: 98% → 2%). Balanced examples carry almost none of the role. The same check finds that code variables are partly shortcut (balanced examples keep 39% of the 3-shot gain) and static lookup mostly format (85%). Table 3, the battery across kotodama-tsumugi's annealed reads, uses four balanced examples.

Static lookup at 0-shot is bare prose with no frame, so its cells mostly show whether a model infers the task's format. All eight models in a check panel gain 19 to 46 points from three worked examples of the item's type. Balanced examples keep most of that gain (28 of 33 points on average). For aliased lists, 0-shot sits close to the balanced reading (7.5 points below it on average) and is a fair floor.
Open-model rows are scored with either vLLM or HF transformers, noted per row and never mixed within a row. A parity check finds the two engines agree within ±.01 accuracy, with no systematic bias.

Answer-deixis cells are calibrated reads over four candidates (me / you / two names), and each model has a strong standing preference (one base answers “me” 59% of the time). A single per-role cell mixes skill with that preference, so a model's three answer columns read together, not one alone.

API rows (Claude and others via OpenRouter) are scored by generation: the first word for reflex, the last word for deliberate. Open models are scored by log-probability over the candidate set. Answer columns use referent scoring for API rows (me/you or the person's name). For open models the name is not a candidate, so me/you is the only way to name the right person.
Deliberate-frame rows on the answer columns are biased toward naming, because the frame says “work out the answer”.
Reflex rows count only calls that used zero reasoning tokens. Some models reason regardless of settings (Qwen3 14B always; gpt-oss and Qwen3 32B often), so their reflex cells are thinner or absent.
API rows were served by whichever OpenRouter provider answered; the provider, and therefore the quantization, is recorded per call.
Set binding with exact-set scoring has no generation version; API rows show single-object sets only.
The human row is a handful of items per cell (two cold reads of a 31- and a 24-item gauntlet): a reference point, not an estimate.
Every open base row is a full vLLM grid. Mistral Large has only a partial reflex row, because of provider failures on the other calls.
